theme: Not by your righteousness; God’s love for the patriarchs
readingInstruction: Read Deuteronomy 9:1-11:32. Moses continues his warning about the danger of self-righteousness. He retells the story of the golden calf, and ends with a call to love and obey. Notice how often he says “not because of your righteousness.”
settingTheScene: Israel is about to cross the Jordan and to defeat nations stronger than themselves. Moses warns them not to think that this is because of their goodness. In fact, they have been “a stubborn people” from the day they left Egypt. He recalls the golden calf, Moses’ intercession, and the second set of tablets. He closes with a call to fear and love the LORD, a promise of blessing, and the first mention of the blessing and curse to be pronounced at Gerizim and Ebal.
observation: “Know therefore that the LORD your God is not giving you this good land to possess because of your righteousness, for you are a stubborn people” (9:6).
“From the day you came out of the land of Egypt until you came to this place, you have been rebellious against the LORD” (9:7).
Moses recounts the forty days on the mountain and the golden calf, and how he fell down before the LORD for forty days and nights (9:9-29).
The LORD wrote the commandments again on two new tablets and put them in the ark (10:1-5).

“And now, Israel, what does the LORD your God require of you, but to fear the LORD your God, to walk in all his ways, to love him, to serve the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul” (10:12).
“Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no longer stubborn” (10:16).
“He executes justice for the fatherless and the widow, and loves the sojourner, giving him food and clothing. Love the sojourner, therefore” (10:18-19).
“Behold, I am setting before you today a blessing and a curse” (11:26).
interpretation:
The centerpiece of this section is the repeated phrase, “not because of your righteousness.” Moses says it again and again. Israel’s coming victory will not be a reward for their goodness. It will be an act of God’s faithfulness to his promise and a judgment on the wickedness of the nations. The land is a gift, and it is an act of grace to a stubborn people.

The retelling of the golden calf is meant to humble. Moses recalls the very worst moment: that at the foot of the mountain where God had just spoken, the people turned to a calf. And he recalls his own intercession, forty days of prostration. Without it, God would have destroyed them. The point is not to shame, but to show that their standing before God depends on his mercy and on a mediator, and not on their record.

Then comes the great question of 10:12: “What does the LORD your God require of you?” The answer is a list, but it is all one thing: fear, walk, love, serve. The center is love. After a long section about rebellion, the call is not to a new set of rules, but to a heart. And God asks this because he has first loved them: “Yet the LORD set his heart in love on your fathers” (10:15).

The command to “circumcise your heart” in 10:16 is one of the most important phrases in the Old Testament. It shows that the real issue was never the outward mark, but the inner condition. Later, Deuteronomy 30:6 promises that God himself will do this, and Jeremiah and Ezekiel pick it up as the promise of the new covenant.

The portrait of God in 10:17-19 is striking. He is “God of gods and Lord of lords,” great and awesome, who takes no bribe, and who loves the sojourner. The most powerful being in the universe is the protector of the powerless. Those who belong to him are to imitate that care.
connection: Paul says, “By grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works” (Ephesians 2:8-9). He writes that “circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit” (Romans 2:29). Jesus said that to love the LORD with all your heart is the great commandment, and that we are to love our neighbor, including the stranger. In Christ, God has given the new heart (Ezekiel 36:26).
application:
Ask where you are tempted to think that blessings come because you deserve them. Replace that thought with gratitude.

Pray 10:12 as a personal prayer. Which of the verbs, fear, walk, love, serve, do you most need this week?

Show practical love to a stranger or someone vulnerable.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that his love for you is not based on your righteousness.
Ask him to circumcise your heart.
Ask him to teach you to fear, walk with, love, and serve him.
